institution: Jyotir-math, one of Śaṅkara's four maṭhs
what_is_said: Life of Śaṅkara: born at Kallady in Travancore, a Nambūri; founded maṭhs for his disciples at Sringeri (south), the Jyotir-math 'vulgo Joshimath' near Badrinath (north), the Śāradā-math at Dvārakā (west) and the Vardhana-math at Puri (east); late in life visited Kashmir, then Badari where he restored the ruined temples of Nārāyaṇ, and died at Kedār aged 32. Four principal disciples whose pupils head the Daśanāmī Daṇḍins.

notes: Textbook four-maṭh statement; nothing on the maṭh's present state (no head, no buildings, not said to be living or vacant). The Joshimath entry in the same author's vol. III (AT12 p. 372-373) does not mention any maṭh.

place: Badrinath (with Joshimath as the Rawal's base)
institution: Badrinath temple and its Rawal (chief priest), linked to Śaṅkara
what_is_said: History chapter (p. 466): Śaṅkara displaced the Buddhist priests of Nārāyaṇa at Badrinath (and of Paśupati at Kedār) and brought in priests from the Dakhin 'whose successors still manage the affairs of those temples'. p. 783: legend that Śaṅkara on his digvijaya found the idols in the Nārada-kuṇḍ and re-established Viṣṇu worship at Badari. p. 787: 'some century and a half ago' (c. 1730s) the worship at Badrinath was conducted by Daṇḍi Paramahaṃsa fakirs from the Dakhin, who gave way to Nambūri ('Lanbiri') Brahmans from Malabar; three or four aspirants to the office of Rawal are always present, one officiating at Badrinath, the rest residing at Joshimath.
quote: Some century and a half ago the worship of Vishnu at Badrinath was conducted by Dandi Paramahansa fakirs from the Dakhin, but these gave way to Dakhini Brahmans of the Lanbiri caste from Kirat Malwaér. There are always three or four aspirants for the office of Rawal, as the chief priest is called, in attendance, one of whom usually takes the duty at Badrinath whilst the remainder reside at Joshimath
notes: Rawal's link to Śaṅkara is given as tradition (Dakhini priests installed by Śaṅkara). The Daṇḍi Paramahaṃsa predecessors are the closest the text comes to a Daśanāmī/Jyotirmaṭh presence; no Śaṅkarācārya of Joshimath is mentioned. Not a maṭh-head: the Rawal is a temple priest.

institution: tradition of Śaṅkarācārya at the Katyūrī capital
what_is_said: The Katyūrī kings first ruled from Joshimath; the temple of Basdeo (Vāsudeva) there is the oldest, Vāsudeva being 'the name given by Sankara' to the supreme being; the Katyūrīs aided Śaṅkara's reforms. One story makes Śaṅkarācārya the unwelcome visitor to the Rani at Joshimath, which the author reads as religious quarrels forcing the dynasty to leave Joshimath for Katyūr.
quote: Another story makes Sankardécharya the unwelcome visitor to the Rani whilst her husband Basdeo was engaged in his ablations at Vishnuprayag. Stripped of its embellishments the story would seem to show that the descendants of Basdeo were obliged to abandon Joshimath owing to religious quarrels
notes: No maṭh mentioned; a Śaṅkara tradition at Joshimath only.

place: Badrinath (with Joshimath as the Rawal's base)
institution: Badrinath temple built by Śaṅkara; Nambūri Rawal
what_is_said: The temple 'said to have been erected some 800 years ago by Sankara Acharya'. Principal priests are Nambūri Brahmans from Malabar; the head priest is the Rawal; a chela of his caste always waits at Joshimath as Rawal-elect. The Rawal has an establishment and under the former Rajas had uncontrolled authority in the temple villages. Offerings c. Rs 5,000 in ordinary years. Joshimath entry (p. 372-373): residences of the Rawal and Badrinath priests, who winter there; no maṭh mentioned.
quote: The principal priests are Namburi Brahmans from Malabar and the head-priest is called Rawal. In order to provide for the succession, in ease of the illness or death of the Rawal, a chela of his caste is always in attendance at Joshimath, so that there is al- ways a Rawal elect present to take possession of the office.
notes: Śaṅkara-Rawal link is implicit (Śaṅkara built the temple; Malabar priests). The Joshimath entry (p. 372-373) is silent on any Śaṅkara maṭh or pīṭha.

notes: Temple ascription to Śaṅkara plus subordination to the Badrinath Rawal; no maṭh. Coded because it ties a Kumaon temple to the Badrinath establishment. Footnote OCR garbled ('This is under the Rawal of Badri i P').

institution: temples at Joshimath and Badrinath founded by Śaṅkara
what_is_said: Śaṅkara purged Kumaon of degraded Buddhism and 're-established the famous temples at Kedarnath, Badrinath and Joshimath'; Viṣṇu worship 're-established in the hills by Sankara Acharya, who founded a temple at Joshimath to Vishnu under the name of Basdeo or Vasudeo, and another at Badrinath'.
quote: His worship was re-established in the hills by Sankara Aeharya, who founded a templo at Joshimath to Vishnu under the name of Basdeo or Vasudeo, and another at Badrinath.
notes: Śaṅkara's foundation at Joshimath is a temple, not a maṭh; the Jyotirmaṭh itself is not named. Almora volume, place in Garhwal.

institution: Badrinath temple at Dwarahat controlled by the Rawal of Badrinath
what_is_said: All the principal temples from Dwarahat westward are ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya; the principal Badrinath temple 'is connected with the greater institution in Garhwal of this name, and is controlled by the Rawal of that place'.
quote: From Dwarahat westward, all the principal temples are ascribed to Sankara A chary a and those here form no exception. The principal temple dedicat¬ ed to Badrinath is connected with the greater institution in Garhwal of this name, and is controlled by the Rawal of that place.
notes: Copies AT12 p. 222 with the footnote brought into the text. RV10 Almora (1981, s.v. Dwarahat) keeps the temple but drops both the Śaṅkara ascription and the Rawal.

institution: the Joshimath monastery founded by Śaṅkara
what_is_said: Śaivism, superseded by Buddhism, owes its restoration to Śaṅkara (fl. c. 7th-8th c.); he introduced Vāsudeva worship, insisted on the Himalayan pilgrimage, 'established the Joshimath monastery and restored the temple at Badrinath, finally proceeding to Kedarnath, where he died at the age of thirty-two'. Pilgrims 50,000-60,000 a year.
quote: He it was too, who insisted upon the efficacy of the pilgrimage to the holy places of the Himalayas. Ho established tho Joshimath monastery and restored the temple at Badriuath, finally proceeding to Kedarnath, where ho died at the age of thirty-two.
notes: The only colonial passage in the north set that names a Joshimath maṭh founded by Śaṅkara outside a four-maṭh list. Said nothing about its present state: the Joshimath entry (p. 168-170) describes the town as winter quarters of the Badrinath Rawal, temples of Narasiṃha, Vishnu etc., and is silent on any maṭh, Śaṅkarācārya or pīṭha (implicitly not a living seat).

institution: Badrinath temple built by Śaṅkara; Nambūri Rawal; estates
what_is_said: Original building 'said to have been erected by Sankara Acharya about the eighth century'. Treasure taken down to Joshimath, the winter headquarters. Endowment: in Almora 45 whole and 26 part villages, gunth revenue Rs 1,750; in Garhwal 164 whole villages and portions of 111 others, Rs 5,429. Rawal chose his successor (Lushington 1846) and received a sanad; 1893 the old Rawal abdicated temporal control; after an 1896 suit (s. 539 CPC) the secular management rests with the Rawal under the Raja of Tehri-Garhwal; the Rawal 'must be a Namburi Brahman from southern India'.
quote: The original building is said to have been erected by Sankara Acharya about the eighth century.
notes: Second quote for the Rawal: 'The Rawal must be a Namburi Brahman from southern Indinj, and a member of the priestly class of his clan' (p. 146). Śaṅkara link only via the temple's foundation; Joshimath as the Rawal's winter seat (p. 168).

institution: Sankaracharya math (= Govardhana maṭha, not so named)
what_is_said: Among the maṭhs clustered round Swarga-dwāra the Kabirpanthi and Śaṅkarācārya maṭhs are prominent; 'the latter math is said to have been founded by Sankaracharya himself', is evidently old (sand dunes all round), and has a fine library of about 1,200 manuscripts, some 300-400 years old. p. 112: over 70 maṭhs in Puri; the chief Śaiva maṭhs in the sandy tract near Swarga-dwār are Śaṅkarācārya, 'with a fine library of old manuscripts', and Sankarananda (branch at Bhubaneswar). p. 97: 'the learned pandit of the Sankaracharya monastery seeking salvation by the way of spiritual knowledge'.
quote: The latter math is said to have been founded by Sankaraoharya himself, and is evidently of considerable age, as the sand, barely kept back by cactus fences, rises all round into a high dune. It has a fine library containing about 1,200 manuscripts, of which some are 300 to 400 years old.
notes: Name 'Govardhana' not used. Hit file dli.ministry.07422 is a partial scan; quote and pages from the full scan in.ernet.dli.2015.206884. Sankarananda maṭh (Śaiva, branch at Bhubaneswar) not coded: no Śaṅkara link stated (RV29 App. III lists it as Dandi Sannyasi). Hunter's Puri (HU19, 1877) has no Śaṅkara maṭh: only unnamed 'little monasteries' at Swarga-dwāra (p. 66).

institution: Gobardhana (Bhogavardhana) Matha, the Sankaracharya Matha
chapter: Places (s.v. Puri: Mathas); also People, Education
what_is_said: Mathas section: 'Gobardhana Matha is one of the oldest in Puri and is believed to have been founded by Adi Sankaracharya in the 9th century'; Gobardhana and Sankarananda are the Śaiva maṭhs near Swargadwara; formerly temple priests were trained at the Sankaracharya Matha and needed its certificate to serve in the Jagannath temple, a function now performed by the Muktimandap (p. 811). p. 774: Sankaracharya Matha prominent at Swargadwara, 'said to have been founded by Sankaracharya'. p. 796: Śaṅkara (788-820) founded the 'Bhogavardhana or Gobardhana Matha at Puri which exists till to[day]'. p. 125: 'He established one of his four Mathas at Puri which still exists.' p. 475, 511: founded the Gobardhana matha 'which is still extant'; Puri's Sanskrit learning traced to him. p. 520: Śrīdhara Svāmin (14th c.) was Mahanta of the 'Govardhana pitha, a famous Sankarite moastery at Puri'. App. III (p. ~844): 'Sankaracharya or Bhogabardhan', Dandi Sannyasi.
quote: Gobardhana Matha is one of the oldest in Puri and is believed to have been founded by Adi Sankaracharya in the 9th century A. D.
notes: Places text at p. 774 reprints BG39 p. 288 (Kabirpanthi and Sankaracharya maṭhs at Swargadwara, Haridasa's grave) but drops the 1,200-MS library. New in 1977: the name Gobardhana/Bhogavardhana, its living status ('still extant'), the Śrīdhara tradition, and the former role in certifying Jagannath priests (now the Muktimaṇḍapa's). No Śaṅkarācārya (head) is named.

institution: Adi Sankar Pravupada Ashram (Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi foundation)
what_is_said: Foundation stone laid 3 March 1973 'at the instance of Shri Jagadguru of Kanchi Kamakoti Peetha'; three temples (Caitanya; Ādi Śaṅkara and his four disciples; Jayadeva with Padmāvatī and Bālakṛṣṇa); managed by the Sankar Bhagavadpada Seva Samiti with liberal donations from the Kāmakoṭi Pīṭha (Rs 1,70,000 for temples and Ashram). 1974-75: 7 boys aged 9-14 taught Sanskrit and the Paippalāda śākhā of the Atharvaveda by 1 full-time and 3 part-time teachers; 7-year course; library.
quote: At the instance of Sbri Jagadguru of Kanchi Kamakoti Peetha, Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, the foundation stone of the Adi Sankar Pravupada Ashram, Puri, was laid on the 3rd March, 1973.
notes: Post-colonial; no colonial antecedent. A Kāñcī institution at the seat-town of Govardhana; the text does not relate it to the Gobardhana Matha.

institution: Sankar Math (founded 1919) and Sankaracharya Chatuspathi
what_is_said: 'The other attraction of Ramrajatala is the Sankar Math near the Ramrajatala railway station founded in 1326 B.S. (A.D. 1919) and named after Jagatguru Sri Sri Sankaracharyya.' p. 465: the Ramrajatala Sankaracharya Chatuspathi is one of the Sanskrit tols recognised by the Vangiya Sanskrit (Shiksha Parishad).
quote: The other attraction of Ramrajatala is the Sankar Math near the Ramrajatala railway station founded in 1326 B.S. (A.D. 1919) and named after Jagatguru Sri Sri Sankaracharyya.
notes: seat=other: a 20th-century maṭh named after Śaṅkara; no affiliation to any of the four seats stated. Not in colonial Howrah texts checked.

institution: Tarakeswar Math (Daśanāmī), held by court to be of the Śaṅkarācārya school
what_is_said: Quoting a court finding: the Daśanāmīs are Vedic Sannyasis, 'the Tarakeswar Math is governed by the Sankaracharya school of thought', and its Mohunt is a Mathadhari Daśanāmī Sannyasi (p. 209). Almost all Daśanāmī maṭhs in Bengal founded by Brahmans from the North-West. p. 726: Mayagiri Dhumrapan appointed Mohanta (1729); subsidiary seats at Guptipara, Nayangarh Bhot-bagan, Baidyabati, Garh Bhavanipur, Santoshpur and Chaipath; Mohanta of Tarakeswar is Mahamandalesvara; the Satis Giri case proved the Daśanāmīs 'Vedic Sannyasis belonging to the school of Sankaracharyya'; 1924 satyagraha; Math declared a public endowment.
quote: Sannyasis belonging to the school of Sankaracharya are Vedic and not Tantric (sic.) Sannyasis, that the Tarakeswar Math is governed by the Sankaracharya school of thought, that the Mohunt of: the Tarakeswar Math...is a Mathadhari Dasanami Sannyasi.
notes: seat=other: a Daśanāmī maṭh tied to Śaṅkara's school by a court ruling, not to a named seat. Not a reprint of BG10 (1912) wording.

institution: Bodh Gaya math of Giri sannyasis (Daśanāmī order 'established by Sankara Acharya')
what_is_said: At the end of the 16th century a Hindu ascetic settled near the ruined temple and founded a maṭh of the Giris, 'one of the seven Saivite orders established by Sankara Acharya'; c. 1727 the Mahanth received the village of Taradih, with the temple ruins, by farman of Muhammad Shah; later disputes with the Buddhists (1890s).
quote: founded a math or monastery of the Hindu sect of Qirs, one of the seven Sai-vite orders established by Sankara Aoharjya.
notes: seat=other: the maṭh itself is not called a Śaṅkara foundation; the Giri order is. Hunter's Gaya (HU12) and the revised Gaya (RV24, 1957) do not repeat the Śaṅkara link for the Bodh Gaya maṭh (RV24 lists 'Sri Mahanth Harihar Gir of Bodh Gaya' among zamindars).

institution: tradition of Śaṅkarācārya and Gaya as a pitṛ-tīrtha
what_is_said: Probably at the end of the 9th century, with the Hindu revival 'due to the efforts of Sankracharya', Gaya was given a place among the five spots of northern India sacred to the manes; also 'a theory that the name Gayawals was given by Shankar'.
quote: It was probably at the end of the ninth century when there was a revival of Hinduism due to the efforts of Sankracharya that Gaya was given a place among the five spots of Northern India sacred to manes
notes: Ādi Śaṅkara tradition only; no institution.

institution: tradition of Śaṅkarācārya's visit to Varanasi
what_is_said: Śaṅkarācārya (c. 8th c.) came from South India to Varanasi to have his monism accepted by the world of scholars (p. 100); even southerners like the great Shankaracharya had to repair to this city (p. 42). No Śaṅkara maṭh in Varanasi is named; maṭhs of Caitanya and Vallabha are.
quote: Shankaracliar)a (circa eighth century A. D.), the great Vedantist philoso- pher, came from South India tO' Varanasi to propound his views and to get his uncompromising monism accepted by the woild of scholaxs
notes: Ādi Śaṅkara (visit tradition). The 1911 Benares volume (UP23 p. 92) only says the restoration of Benares 'began with the itinerant preaching of Shankaracharya'; Atkinson's Benares (AT14 p. 56-57) lists 'Shankaracharya' among Śaiva sects with no maṭh. The Bhinga Dandi Ashram (1924, p. 386) is not linked to a Śaṅkarācārya.

institution: visit of the Sringeri Śaṅkarācārya to Nagpur
what_is_said: 'The successor in office of Sankar Acharya, the spiritual head of the Saivite Hindus of all India, who lives at Sringeri in Madras, visited Nagpur some two or three years ago' (c. 1903-04); the Kalankī Brahmans petitioned him to be allowed to marry other Brahmans and he is believed to have agreed, but no intermarriage has followed.
quote: When the successor in office of Sankar Acharya, the spiritual head of the Saivite Hindus of all India, who lives at Sringeri in Madras, visited Nagpur some two or t hree years ago, it is believed that the KalankI Brahmans submitted a petition to him that they might be allowed to marry
notes: Wardha volume reporting a visit to neighbouring Nagpur. A dated tour of a living Śaṅkarācārya in the Central Provinces.

institution: village named after Śaṅkarācārya's sojourn
what_is_said: Village at the junction of the Hiran and Narmada, 18 miles NE of Narsinghpur; name derived from 'the well-known saint Sankara Charya, who is said to have sojourned here'; fair in Kārttik and Makar Saṅkrānti bathing (c. 5,000).
quote: The name is supposed to be derived from that of the well-known saint Sankara Charya, who is said to have sojourned here.
notes: Ādi Śaṅkara tradition; file is the backup scan in.ernet.dli.2015.206912 of CP06.

institution: local 'shankaracharya' with caste jurisdiction
what_is_said: Brahmans have a dharmādhikārī (hereditary; nine in Basim town alone) and 'a shankaracharya with power to punish for breaches of caste rule'; the shankaracharya 'requires to be personally qualified for his post'.
quote: Brahmans have also a dharmadhikari, who is a final authority on questions of religion, and a shankara- charya with power to punish for breaches of caste rule and the like; the dharmadhtkari holds his office by hereditary right, but should take skilled advice if he is himself unlearned ; there are nine representatives in the single town of Basim ; the shankaracharya requires to be personally qualified for his post
notes: Probably a local deputy of a Śaṅkarācārya (cf. Karvīr/Saṅkeśvar agents in Berar), but no seat named; not a maṭh.

institution: samādhi of a Śaṅkarācārya (Vidyāśaṅkara Bhāratī) and temple of Shankaracharya Swami
what_is_said: Nirmal is sacred for its liṅga and, by tradition, 'the samadhi of one of the great Shankaracharyas'; of eight temples built c. 1750 by Shankraji Keshav (Maratha Subhedar of Vasai) one is dedicated to Shankaracharya Swami, with an annual Government grant, managed by a committee; a week-long fair (c. 6,000 pilgrims from Thane, Raigad, Bombay, Gujarat) on the death anniversary of 'the eighth Shankaracharya Vidyashankar Bharati', Kārttik vadya 11 (p. 1035). s.v. Sopara (p. 1056-57): the great temple of Shankaracharya Swami on Nirmal hill raised by Shankarji Keshav Phadke after the fall of the Portuguese (1739).
quote: according to tradition, the place where stands the samadhi of one of the great Shankaracharyas, the apostle of the modern Brahmanic system.
